query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor alloying addition of Zr (3–7 at.%) into a eutectic AlCoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy, processed via controlled thermomechanical treatment, will both increase tensile yield strength and enhance room-temperature ductility by refining the lamellar colony spacing and improving interfacial cohesion.
generation.material_initial_state: The baseline eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibits a dual-phase lamellar microstructure with relatively coarse colony spacing and weak interfacial bonding, which makes it prone to microcrack initiation under tensile load.
generation.intervention: Minor alloying addition of Zr (3–7 at.%) introduced during alloy synthesis followed by standard casting and controlled thermomechanical processing (e.g., hot rolling plus cold rolling) to achieve a well-defined dual-phase lamellar structure.
generation.conditions: Alloys will be prepared with low Zr content (3–7 at.%), using conventional casting techniques followed by hot rolling (e.g., 50% reduction) and subsequent cold rolling (e.g., 70% reduction) and rapid annealing to ensure a refined lamellar microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: The Zr addition induces localized lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening which refines the lamellar colony spacing and enhances the interfacial bonding between the dual phases.
generation.mechanism: The addition of Zr, having a larger atomic radius, creates local lattice distortions that act as obstacles to dislocation motion (solid solution strengthening), while simultaneously promoting a finer, more continuous lamellar colony structure that redistributes local stresses and mitigates the nucleation and propagation of microcracks at internal boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the Zr-doped alloy is expected to exhibit higher tensile yield strength due to solid solution strengthening and enhanced ductility at room temperature as a result of improved interfacial cohesion and refined microstructural features that delay microcrack initiation.
generation.baseline: The unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with coarser lamellar colonies and weak interfacial boundaries typically experiences a trade-off between strength and ductility, showing brittleness during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the intervention is expected to hold within the designed Zr content range (3–7 at.%), under conventional casting and thermomechanical processing conditions that preserve the dual-phase lamellar microstructure. Deviations outside this range or significant alterations in processing may yield different phases or microstructures, thereby altering the mechanical response.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence in related MEAs supports improvements with Zr additions, the exact quantitative increases in yield strength and ductility (and their balance) in eutectic high-entropy alloys remain to be determined experimentally. Variations in processing conditions could also affect the final microstructure and its mechanical responses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the eutectic AlCoCrFeNi alloy with 0, 3, 5, and 7 at.% Zr using controlled casting followed by a standard thermomechanical treatment (hot rolling 50% followed by cold rolling 70% and rapid annealing). Measure microstructural features (lamellar spacing, interfacial quality) using electron microscopy and perform room-temperature tensile tests to assess yield strength and ductility.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Lamellar colony spacing and interfacial characteristics (via SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-doped alloys (within 3–7 at.%) do not demonstrate both a significant increase in tensile yield strength and an improvement in ductility relative to the undoped baseline, or if microcrack initiation is not mitigated (as evidenced by similar or inferior interfacial structures), then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Most medium entropy alloys (MEAs) exhibit excellent mechanical properties, but their applications are limited because of their high density. This study explores a series of lightweight nonequiatomic Ti65(AlCrNbV)35-xZrx (x = 3, 5, 7, and 10) MEAs with a low density, high strength, and high ductility. To achieve solid solution strengthening, Zr with a large atomic radius was used. In addition, various thermomechanical treatment parameters were adopted to further improve the MEAs’ mechanical properties. The density of the MEAs was revealed to be approximately 5 g/cm3, indicating that they were lightweight. Through an X-ray diffraction analysis, the MEAs were revealed to have a single body-centered cubic structure not only in the as-cast state but also after thermomechanical treatment. In terms of mechanical properties, all the as-cast MEAs with Zr additions achieved excellent performance (>1000 MPa tensile yield strength and 20% tensile ductility). In addition, hot rolling effectively eliminated the defects of the MEAs; under a given yield strength, hot-rolled MEAs exhibited superior ductility relative to non-hot-rolled MEAs. Studies of lightweight Ti-rich MEAs [] have explored finetuned Ti65(AlCrNbV)35 alloy compositions and have added various amounts of atomic radius zirconium (Zr) to enhance the mechanical properties of these MEAs through substitutional solid solution strengthening. To further improve the mechanical properties of these MEAs, two thermomechanical processing routes have been tested; the first is cold rolling 70% (CR70) followed by rapid annealing, and the second is hot rolling 50% plus cold rolling 70% (HR50CR70) followed by rapid annealing. In addition, the relationship between the rapid annealing temperature and the microstructure and mechanical properties of MEAs was investigated.

proposals.intervention: Incorporate controlled hydrogen charging during processing
proposals.conditions: Expose the cast alloy to a controlled hydrogen atmosphere (e.g., via electrochemical charging) at room temperature prior to tensile testing, with hydrogen concentration optimized to avoid embrittlement (targeting low-to-moderate levels)
proposals.structural_mediator: Reduction of stacking fault energy leading to enhanced nanotwin formation at lamellar colony boundaries
proposals.mechanism: Hydrogen lowers the stacking fault energy, promoting the formation of nanotwins during deformation. These twins can arrest or blunt microcrack propagation at the internal colony boundaries, thereby simultaneously increasing strain hardening (strength) and accommodating plastic deformation (ductility)
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified lamellar baseline, the hydrogen-charged EHEA is expected to exhibit higher tensile yield strength and improved tensile elongation due to the onset of twin-induced plasticity and the mitigation of microcrack initiation
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention directly targets the dual problem of high strength and brittle microcrack initiation by activating a deformation mechanism (nanotwinning) that enhances ductility without sacrificing strength, thereby overcoming the usual strength‐ductility trade-off in eutectic HEAs

proposals.material_system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy based on AlCoCrFeNi with minor Zr addition
proposals.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition of a large atomic radius element (Zr)
proposals.conditions: Prepare alloys with low Zr content (e.g., 3–7 at.%) via conventional casting followed by controlled thermomechanical processing (e.g., hot rolling) to achieve a well‐defined dual‐phase lamellar structure
proposals.structural_mediator: Solid solution strengthening plus lattice distortion that refines the lamellar colony spacing and enhances interfacial cohesion
proposals.mechanism: The addition of Zr creates localized lattice distortions that not only strengthen the phases via solid solution effects but also refine the spacing and continuity of the lamellar colonies. This refinement promotes a more uniform stress distribution at internal boundaries and suppresses microcrack nucleation
proposals.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the Zr-doped EHEA will display increased tensile yield strength and improved room-temperature ductility as the refined microstructure mitigates crack initiation and propagation while maintaining intrinsic phase ductility
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By leveraging a single alloying addition that both strengthens the matrix and refines the lamellar architecture, this approach aims to sidestep the typical trade-off between strength and ductility in eutectic HEAs

proposals.intervention: Apply a rapid post-casting annealing treatment near the eutectoid decomposition temperature
proposals.conditions: Subject as-cast eutectic samples to rapid annealing at ~700–750 °C for 30–50 seconds with a high heating rate (~15 K/s) followed by quenching to room temperature
proposals.structural_mediator: Partial decomposition or 'rejuvenation' of the lamellar colonies resulting in the formation of finely spaced nano-twins and a modified interlamellar architecture
proposals.mechanism: Rapid annealing induces a controlled transient phase transformation that slightly alters the lamellar interface chemistry and structure, promoting reversible formation of nano-twins and enhancing local plasticity. This process softens potential crack initiation sites while preserving strength through phase refinement
proposals.predicted_outcome: The annealed alloy is expected to show an improved balance, with higher tensile yield strength along with increased ductility compared to the unmodified (as-cast) dual-phase lamellar microstructure
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single thermal processing intervention re-engineers the internal boundaries of the lamellar colonies to prevent microcrack nucleation while activating energy-dissipating deformation modes, thereby breaking the conventional inverse relationship between strength and ductility

proposals.intervention: Implement a localized laser surface treatment to modify colony boundaries
proposals.conditions: Apply a controlled laser surface melting process using precise laser power and scanning speed to create a thin, rapidly solidified surface layer while leaving the bulk lamellar microstructure intact
proposals.structural_mediator: Modification of the interfacial regions between lamellar colonies by forming a refined, columnar or composite-like structure with enhanced interfacial bonding
proposals.mechanism: The laser treatment selectively melts and rapidly resolidifies the near-surface region, thereby engineering the internal boundaries to become less prone to microcrack initiation. The altered microstructure at the boundaries changes crack propagation paths and facilitates crack bridging or blunting during tensile deformation
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated samples, the laser-surface-treated EHEA is predicted to show improved tensile strength (due to a more robust interfacial bonding) along with enhanced ductility from the crack-deflecting microstructure at the colony boundaries
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention targets the critical role of colony boundaries in microcrack initiation, using a single, localized processing step to re-engineer these interfaces so as to improve both strength and ductility simultaneously without altering the bulk lamellar architecture

decision.rationale: Candidate A proposes a single alloying intervention by adding a minor amount of a large atomic radius element (Zr) into the eutectic high‐entropy alloy. This strategy is supported by evidence from analogous Ti-rich MEAs where Zr addition has promoted solid solution strengthening while refining the microstructural features (e.g., lamellar spacing) that are critical for mediating stress at the internal colony boundaries. In contrast to the other proposals, this approach directly addresses the dual constraints of strength and ductility by modifying the phase morphology and interfacial properties in one step. While thermal treatments and hydrogen charging also affect microstructural evolution, they come with potential drawbacks (e.g., process uniformity or embrittlement risks) that are less problematic for a controlled minor alloying addition. Thus, we adopt direction A.
